news.content: Skip to content Skip to search AUSTRALIA’S NATIONAL SCIENCE AGENCY About Research Work with us Careers Education News Events Search Quick links Climate change COVID-19 research Diets Staff profiles Our Centenary story As we mark our centenary in 2026, our story is not one but many, told over generations through science in the service of our nation, and beyond. Our legacy We are CSIRO Your national science agency We deliver the science Australians need for the nation they want – productive, sustainable, healthy and secure. Our Vision Work with us Science and technology can help your business Spanning a range of scientific disciplines across the various stages of the innovation lifecycle, we apply our research to inform policy, develop new industries and evolve existing sectors. Unlock success Innovation Innovation for impact Our suite of innovation, funding and entrepreneurship programs give researchers and industry the opportunity to collaborate on projects that help solve Australia’s greatest challenges. Discover how we can help We recognise that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples make extraordinary contributions to Australian life including in cultural, economic and scientific domains. Acknowledgement of Country CSIRO acknowledges the Traditional Owners of the lands, seas and waters, of the area that we live and work on across Australia and pays its respect to Elders past and present. Indigenous science projects Solving the greatest challenges Look around: that’s CSIRO science making a difference Most Australians encounter CSIRO science every day, often before breakfast. Expert Commentary: What do we know about H5 bird flu? Following the arrival of H5 bird flu in Australia, scientists from CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) explain what their testing has told us about the virus. The decades‐old ‘AI alignment problem’ has finally become a reality. Solving it won’t be easy Alignment cannot depend on one AI becoming perfectly trustworthy. Our greatest inventions Fast Wifi Aerogard Hendra vaccine Plastic banknotes Raft Polymerisation Fast Wifi Our wireless invention lies at the heart of what is now the most popular way to connect computers without wires. It is used in offices, public buildings, homes and coffee shops - often called 'WiFi Hotspots'. The invention came out of our pioneering work in radioastronomy. Where did wifi come from? Aerogard Aerogard has been keeping flying pests at bay since the 1960s, helping prevent diseases that infect animals and humans. In 1938, Doug Waterhouse was working on a repellent for sheep blowfly. With the arrival of World War II, he turned to protecting allied troops from mosquitoes. Itching to learn more World's first Hendra vaccine In 1994, a deadly new virus threatened to stop Australia's premier horse race – the Melbourne Cup. Over 16 years, 18 outbreaks of Hendra virus were recorded. In May 2011, we announced the development of a prototype vaccine for horses. By March 2013, our scientists confirmed that horses were immune to Hendra virus six months post vaccination. How it happened Plastic banknotes Australia's introduction of plastic bank notes with optically variable devices (OVDs), developed by CSIRO, was a world's first and represented a paradigm shift towards a currency secure against forgery. This was one of our longest and most successful research initiatives. Learn more about our inventions RAFT polymerisation RAFT polymerisation is a new technique for creating plastics that allows a higher degree of control over the way molecules link together. Plastics are essential elements of modern life, created through the process of polymerisation to give them a range of different attributes. Learn more Latest news There are no news releases to show. The report does not include specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, focusing instead on the implications of the virus for public health and scientific research. The commentary is based on the ACDP's ongoing work and does not mention any current containment or response measures. The report serves as an informative overview of the virus and its relevance to Australia's scientific and health sectors.

How would we know? Published: August 16, 2026 4:05pm EDT Bird flu is circulating among birds on the Australian mainland. So with the confirmed number of detections growing, you may be wondering about the risk of birds infecting humans. So far in 2026, no humans in Australia have been diagnosed with the currently circulating strain. And evidence from overseas indicates that in the rare situation this would occur, illness would generally be mild. But not everyone with flu-like symptoms gets tested. And even if they did, a general flu test cannot distinguish between bird flu and seasonal flu. So how would we know if a human caught bird flu from an infected bird? What is bird flu? What’s changed? Bird flu (or avian influenza) refers to strains of flu viruses that mainly affect birds. The current strain of concern is known as H5N1. Since 2020, a sub-strain of H5N1, known as 2.3.4.4b, has been circulating around the world. This has resulted in the deaths of millions of birds (including poultry). It has also crossed into other species, including dairy cows in the United States, and marine mammals. Distressingly, mass mortality events – where many animals die suddenly – have been reported. In June, the first cases of H5N1 influenza were reported in Australia, first in migratory birds, then in local wild birds. Now, the government does not report case numbers, just events, where one or more birds may be involved. There has been at least one mass mortality event reported in Australia. So with more bird flu now circulating in Australia, can we expect more humans to be infected? Yes, humans can catch bird flu Since 2003, the World Health Organization (WHO) has reported 1,000 cases of H5N1 bird flu in humans globally, with 479 deaths. This year, it has reported seven cases of H5N1 bird flu in humans (in Cambodia, Bangladesh and India) with two deaths. However, 2.3.4.4b – the sub-strain currently circulating globally, including Australia – seems to generally cause mild disease in humans. However, there have been a few cases of more severe 2.3.4.4b disease (including two deaths in the US). To date, there have been no human cases of 2.3.4.4b in Australia. But there was one case of a related H5N1 strain, 2.3.2.1a, in a child who returned from overseas travel. Even with more 2.3.4.4b circulating in recent weeks, the Australian Centre for Disease Control still assesses the risk to humans as low. While humans can catch the virus from close contact with infected birds, the virus does not currently spread between humans. This means the risk of a significant human pandemic – which would need widespread transmission between humans – is currently low. Who’s at risk? What are the symptoms? Experience in other countries suggests most human infection results from close contact with infected animals. In Australia, the highest risk groups currently are wildlife carers, including veterinary staff and those managing sick or dead birds. But public health authorities are watching for other groups who may become at risk should the outbreak spread, such as poultry workers. Symptoms are typically mild, with a runny dose, cough and fever, and sometimes nausea and diarrhoea. Conjunctivitis (“pink eye”) is one symptom associated with bird flu that we don’t often see in seasonal flu. However, more serious disease can develop. In other countries, this has generally been associated with infections due to H5N1 strains other than 2.3.4.4b. Is there a bird flu test? What happens next? Standard flu tests should detect bird flu too. But they don’t distinguish between seasonal flu and bird flu. Detecting bird flu relies on doctors letting the lab know they suspect bird flu (for example, if a patient has had contact with birds that may be infected). So if you have flu-like symptoms and are in one of the groups more likely to be exposed to bird flu, tell your doctor so they can order the specific test for bird flu. It’s best to phone ahead, and present for testing wearing a mask. People with confirmed bird flu should be monitored and follow the directions of their local public health unit. Authorities will also assess whether others may have been exposed and infected. Some people may be offered the preventive antiviral medicine oseltamivir to reduce their risk of becoming infected or to treat an infection. How else would we know? There is also surveillance for bird flu in humans. This means actively looking out for signals without relying on individuals coming forward for testing. For instance, the WHO Collaborating Centre for Reference and Research on Influenza in Melbourne tests a selection of isolates (samples) routinely sent from other laboratories. Other ways to look out for humans infected with bird flu include surveillance systems based in selected hospitals and general practices. What precautions can I take? If you work with birds, advice is available about the right type of personal protective equipment to use to minimise your risk of infection. Washing your hands is also important. A regular seasonal flu vaccine is recommended for people at risk. This is not to protect against bird flu but to prevent people becoming sick with both seasonal and bird flu viruses at the same time. If you notice sick or dead birds, or other animals, you should: avoid touching them; record your location and what you see (take photos or video, if possible); report this to the 24-hour Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. As of August 16, 2026, no human cases of the currently circulating strain, 2.3.4.4b, have been reported in Australia, though there was one case of a related H5N1 strain (2.3.2.1a) in a child who returned from overseas travel. The Australian Centre for Disease Control assesses the risk to humans as low, emphasizing that while humans can contract bird flu through close contact with infected birds, the virus does not spread between humans. Public health authorities are actively monitoring for potential human infections and have established surveillance systems in hospitals and general practices. They also advise individuals who may have been exposed to report sick or dead birds and take precautions such as handwashing and using appropriate personal protective equipment. The article highlights the importance of specific testing for bird flu and the need for vigilance among high-risk groups, including wildlife carers and poultry workers.

news.content_title: ‘It’s definitely going to happen’: NT prepares for H5N1 bird flu
news.content: The highly contagious H5N1 strain of bird flu is expected to reach the Northern Territory soon, the Environment Department has said, with staff sampling faeces and water supplies to identify contamination. The ABC reported NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment senior director of species management Tony Griffiths said combating H5N1 in the NT would largely be based on surveying areas such as the Top End coastline and Barkly lakes and using bird enthusiasts to be on the lookout. “It’s definitely going to happen. It could be weeks, it could be months, but it’s a national event, it’s the biggest national disease event that has ever occurred in Australia for wildlife,” Dr Griffiths told ABC News. The flu was first detected in Western Australia in late June and has now been found in all six states. Dr Griffiths said department staff had been sampling faeces and water supplies to identify contamination, but they were not going to vaccinate native species. “We have 450 species of bird in the Territory and 37 of those are threatened, but we don’t rely on captive breeding programs to support the management of those species,” Dr Griffiths said. “The threatened birds we have are dispersed over very large areas and it’s very difficult to catch them to vaccinate.” NT chief veterinary officer Sue Fitzpatrick told the ABC backyard poultry farmers and other bird owners need to watch out for the disease. “We’re looking for bird keepers to protect their birds from wild birds, enclose their runs and put some roof over their runs, protect feed and water sources from wild birds,” Dr Fitzpatrick said

news.content_zh: 北领地 (NT) 正在为 H5N1 禽流感病毒的到来做好准备,该病毒已在澳大利亚所有六个州被发现。环境部通过其高级主管托尼·格里菲斯(Tony Griffiths)警告说,这种菌株预计很快就会到达北领地,并强调这是全国范围内最大的野生动物疾病事件。工作包括对粪便和供水进行采样,以及依靠鸟类爱好者来监测污染迹象。Griffiths 博士指出,北领地有 450 种鸟类,其中 37 种受到威胁,但由于后勤方面的挑战,本地物种的 疫苗接种 没有计划。北领地首席兽医官 Sue Fitzpatrick 博士敦促散养家禽​​养殖户采取预防措施,例如封闭鸟道并保护饲料和水源免受 野生鸟类 的影响。目前情况仍在调查中,北领地尚未报告确诊病例。应对措施的重点是 监测 和社区意识,而不是直接干预。

How will this protect them? Published: August 18, 2026 1:18am EDT A major push is underway to catch and vaccinate more than 5,000 little penguins in Victoria to protect them against the virulent H5N1 bird flu. Victorian wildlife officers will carry out vaccinations at little penguin colonies at Phillip Island and St Kilda, in what the state government says is the world’s largest program to target wild birds. One little penguin at Phillip Island has already died of bird flu. Capturing wildlife for vaccination is difficult, particularly because they may need two or more doses of the vaccine. So, how will this unprecedented program help little penguins? A significant threat Little penguins (Eudyptula minor) are the world’s smallest penguin, reaching a height of about 30 centimetres and weighing around 1.5 kilograms. These charismatic birds live on the southern coast of Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales, as well as Tasmania and New Zealand. Famously, they can be found on Philip Island in Victoria, where more than 700,000 people come each year to see them emerge from the ocean at sunset and waddle up the beach to their burrows in the “penguin parade”. The colonies at Philip Island and St Kilda are home to around 40,000 penguins. Because large numbers of birds live close together and the virus is highly infectious, bird flu poses a significant threat. These little penguins live in burrows in the coastal health at Phillip Island. Goddard_Photography/Getty Capturing wildlife to vaccinate them is difficult, particularly because the bird flu vaccination requires they be caught twice, for two doses. However, little penguins are flightless, live in colonies and return at night to the same burrow, making them easier to capture and vaccinate. Birds affected by H5N1 may be unable to stand or fly, or may appear lethargic. They may have an unusual head or neck posture, or die suddenly in large numbers without any signs at all. Little penguins are already under pressure from invasive predators such as cats and foxes, artificial light, roads and overfishing. Climate change is also taking a toll, with warming oceans reducing fish numbers. A popular tourist attraction in Bicheno, Tasmania, recently had to temporarily close due to adults failing to return to shore and abandoning chicks. Ecologists believed it was linked to a sudden rise in sea temperature. Other birds also being vaccinated While the scale of Victoria’s vaccination program of wild birds is unprecedented, New Zealand – the land of birds – is also vaccinating around 300 captive (or flightless) individuals from five species. These include the critically endangered kākāpō (Strigops habroptilus), and endangered South Island takahē (Porphyrio hochstetteri). Endangered captive birds in Australian zoos are being vaccinated too, including the regent honeyeater (Anthochaera phrygia), orange-bellied parrot (Neophema chrysogaster) and Western Australia’s black cockatoos. The federal government recently authorised the use of H5N1 vaccines for priority native bird species. The inactivated viral vaccine (made of dead virus particles) had not been tested on any native birds, much less little penguins, until recently. Why two doses are needed Just like many of the vaccines we humans receive, this H5N1 vaccine requires a booster shot. After the initial vaccination, the vaccinated animal’s immune system can detect foreign viral particles and develop antibodies. The first vaccine shot also produces specialised cells called memory B cells, which remember the protein makeup of the virus when they meet it again. A second or booster vaccine is often required as part of a vaccination regime, typically after several weeks. This leads to a rapid increase in the number of antibody molecules in the blood because the memory B cells recognise the virus and trigger a wave of antibody production. Having higher levels of antibodies in the blood increases the chances of them locating a virus in the blood stream, ultimately stopping the virus infecting the penguin. Vaccines essential to response Vaccines are not guaranteed to prevent an infection every time, and we cannot vaccinate all the penguins. But they are an important tools we can use to reduce the impact of bird flu on precious wildlife, and protect other animals. The bird flu virus will continue to evolve and adapt to outsmart the host immune systems, much like COVID. Climate change will put even more stress on wildlife and induce virus adaption. Over time, new vaccines will need to be developed for new virus strains. For now, bird flu is here and vaccines are an essential part of the fight. Please not approach or touch birds that are unwell or dead. Report to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline (1800 675 888). Vaccination Avian flu H5N1 Environment Avian flu Bird flu Want to write? analysis.location_and_population: Victoria, Australia; Phillip Island and St Kilda penguin colonies; target population: more than 5,000 little penguins (Eudyptula minor); colonies total ~40,000 penguins.
analysis.event: Victoria’s state government is conducting the world’s largest vaccination program against H5N1 avian influenza in wild little penguins, using an inactivated viral vaccine requiring two doses per bird.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: One confirmed death of a little penguin from H5N1 reported at Phillip Island; large colonies (~40,000 penguins) at high risk due to high infectivity and close living conditions; penguins already stressed by invasive predators, artificial light, roads, overfishing, and climate-driven reductions in fish.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Vaccination program ongoing; wildlife officers capturing and vaccinating penguins; vaccine not yet tested on little penguins prior to this program; requires two doses with weeks between; vaccines reduce impact but cannot prevent all infections; virus expected to evolve, necessitating future vaccine updates; public advised not to approach sick or dead birds and to report sightings to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline.

analysis.brief_en: Victoria, Australia, has launched the world’s largest wild-bird vaccination campaign against H5N1 avian influenza, targeting more than 5,000 little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda. The state government-led effort uses an inactivated H5N1 vaccine that requires two doses per bird, a strategy previously untested on little penguins. One fatality from H5N1 has already been confirmed at Phillip Island, where colonies of around 40,000 penguins face heightened risk due to dense living conditions and multiple environmental stressors. Wildlife officers are capturing and vaccinating the birds, but logistical challenges remain, including the need for repeat captures. Experts note that while vaccines can reduce impact, H5N1 is likely to evolve, requiring ongoing vaccine development. The public is urged not to touch sick or dead birds and to report sightings to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline.

Photograph: ozflash/Getty Images/iStockphoto View image in fullscreen Authorities had been racing to vaccinate 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island before the first confirmed case of H5 bird flu in the colony. Photograph: ozflash/Getty Images/iStockphoto First Australian death of little penguin with H5 bird flu confirmed on Phillip Island Authorities confirm first Australian death of species found with virus near where it attracts crowds to a ‘penguin parade’ Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Australia’s first case of the deadly H5 bird flu in a little penguin has been confirmed on Victoria’s Phillip Island, only days after the state government announced it would begin vaccinating the species. Confirmation of the virus in the little penguin will spark a race to vaccinate thousands of birds, with the government announcing on Saturday it would begin the rollout on Monday. The government did not provide the exact location where the bird was found, but said it was not inside the island’s famous penguin parade area. A spokesperson confirmed the little penguin had died. There are about 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island, making it the world’s biggest colony of the species and a major tourist attraction. Bird flu has been evolving and migrating for 30 years. It is a far more deadly virus that has now arrived in Australia Read more Environment advocates have been concerned about the potential for mass deaths of little penguins if the virus reached the island. Euan Ritchie, a professor in wildlife ecology and conservation at Deakin university, said the detection of H5 bird flu in the much-loved little penguin population was “devastating”. “Phillip Island is home to a diverse array and significant populations of native wildlife, including Australian fur seals, eastern barred bandicoots, and recently reintroduced bush stone curlews,” he said. “Governments must provide whatever resources are needed to help wildlife survive through and recover from this bird flu outbreak.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email On Wednesday, the Victorian government announced plans for the world’s largest H5 bird flu vaccination program of wild birds. The government said it would vaccinate up to 5,000 little penguins across populations at Phillip Island and at Melbourne’s St Kilda beach. While vaccinating wild birds is challenging, it was considered possible in Victoria’s wild little penguins because they generally return to the same burrows at Phillip Island and St Kilda each night. But vaccination requires the delivery of two doses with a gap of a few weeks between each dose. The detection on Phillip Island will spark concern that it may be too late for some little penguins to develop immunity. Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said he understood Victorians would be worried about the detection of the deadly virus in a little penguin. “We know that the detection in a little penguin on Phillip Island is of concern,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion “But we are proceeding with vaccination of the little penguin colony on Phillip Island and at St Kilda as a meaningful way in which it can help mitigate the impact of H5 on those populations. “We know that little penguins are iconic and highly valued by Victorians, and for that reason, we are working as a priority to protect those colonies.” The state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said Agriculture Victoria and Phillip Island Nature Parks “activated plans” to vaccinate little penguins as soon as the federal government authorised the vaccines for priority native bird species. “Agriculture Victoria is working closely with Phillip Island Nature Parks to support vaccination of little penguins from Monday,” he said. “While the first detection in a little penguin is a concern, vaccination of little penguins on Phillip Island remains a meaningful way to help protect this important colony.” The Victorian government said there had been two further detections of H5 in greater crested terns, one at Lakes Entrance and the other at Dromana on the Mornington peninsula. Todd said the Lakes Entrance detection was significant because it showed the virus was continuing to move through wild bird populations across Victoria. On Saturday, the NSW government also confirmed the fifth detected case in the state, in a tern found at Eden on the far south coast. The government said it would increase surveillance in the area as a result. There have been two other confirmed cases in local birds in the state, one at Narooma on the state’s south coast and one at Wentworth in the far south-west. All of the confirmed cases in local birds have been in greater crested terns. analysis.event: First confirmed Australian death of a little penguin infected with H5 avian influenza virus reported by authorities; vaccination program for little penguins initiated.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: One confirmed death of a little penguin; approximately 40,000 little penguins in the Phillip Island colony; two further detections of H5 in greater crested terns in Victoria (Lakes Entrance and Dromana); fifth case in New South Wales (Eden); risk of mass mortality in little penguin colony acknowledged.

analysis.brief_en: Australia confirmed its first case of H5 avian influenza in a little penguin on Phillip Island, Victoria, marking the country’s first recorded death of the species from the virus. The discovery has triggered an emergency vaccination campaign targeting up to 5,000 little penguins across Phillip Island and Melbourne’s St Kilda beach, with doses spaced weeks apart. Authorities also reported two additional H5 detections in greater crested terns in Victoria and a fifth case in New South Wales, raising concerns about wider spread among wild bird populations. While the infected penguin was found outside the popular ‘penguin parade’ area, experts warn the colony of roughly 40,000 birds faces significant risk if immunity cannot be established in time. The Victorian government emphasized the iconic status of the species and pledged priority resources to protect the colony as vaccination efforts begin.

While the infected penguin was found outside the popular ‘penguin parade’ area, experts warn the colony of roughly 40,000 birds faces significant risk if immunity cannot be established in time. news.title_zh: 菲利普岛确认澳大利亚首例小企鹅感染 H5 禽流感死亡 - 卫报
news.source_body_en: Australia confirmed its first case of H5 avian influenza in a little penguin on Phillip Island, Victoria, marking the country’s first recorded death of the species from the virus. The discovery has triggered an emergency vaccination campaign targeting up to 5,000 little penguins across Phillip Island and Melbourne’s St Kilda beach, with doses spaced weeks apart. news.content_zh: 澳大利亚在维多利亚州菲利普岛的一只小企鹅身上确认了首例 H5 禽流感 病例,这是该国首次有记录的该物种因该病毒死亡。这一发现引发了一项紧急 疫苗接种 运动,目标是菲利普岛和墨尔本圣基尔达海滩上的多达 5,000 只小企鹅,服药间隔数周。当局还报告在维多利亚州的大凤头燕鸥中检测到另外两例 H5 病例,在新南威尔士州检测到第五例病例,引发了人们对 野生鸟类 人群中更广泛传播的担忧。虽然受感染的企鹅是在受欢迎的“企鹅游行”区域外发现的,但专家警告说,如果不能及时建立免疫力,大约 40,000 只企鹅的栖息地将面临重大风险。维多利亚州政府强调了该物种的标志性地位,并承诺在 疫苗接种 工作开始时优先提供资源来保护该群体。

South Atlantic News Agency MercoPress, en Español Montevideo, August 20th 2026 - 20:56 UTC A personalized mRNA therapy passes a phase 3 melanoma trial for the first time Harry and Meghan will move to the UK without resuming official royal duties Falklands consolidates the future of its economy in the fishing and hydrocarbons industries Discover more War & Conflict Multilateral Organizations political News Geographic Reference History Newspapers Latinos & Latin-Americans Politics news Australia launches program to vaccinate colonies of little penguins against avian influenza Wednesday, August 19th 2026 - 08:45 UTC Full article 0 comments Operations will be conducted at night when the penguins return from the sea and are directed to a special area where they will receive the first dose According to ABC News Australia wildlife conservation agencies in the state of Victoria have launched a program to vaccinate little penguins against the H5 strain of avian influenza. Over the next few weeks, experts plan to capture and vaccinate more than 5,000 birds in colonies on Philip Island and St. Kilda. The virus, first detected in southwestern Victoria about two and a half weeks ago, has spread to Philip Island. On the eve of the vaccination campaign, the death of a little penguin from the virus was confirmed. The bird was found in a different part of the island, away from the site of the nightly tourist penguin watch. The colony on Phillip Island numbers up to 40,000 birds and is one of the largest in the world. A state government study released in May 2025 modeled the risks of H5N1 to this population and predicted that, in a worst-case scenario, between 8,000 and 16,000 penguins could die. Little penguins are vulnerable to the spread of infection because they nest and gather in large groups. Victoria’s Chief Biodiversity Officer, James Todd, stated that operations will be conducted at night. When the penguins return from the sea, they will be directed to a special area where they will receive their first dose of the vaccine and be microchipped, after which the birds will be able to return to their burrows. The number of staff will be limited to reduce biosafety risks to both people and animals. According to Todd, vaccinating wild animals is complicated by the need for two doses of the vaccine, which is usually impractical or impossible. Priority will be given to penguins participating in the tourist “penguin parade”: they are accustomed to people and have predictable movement patterns. The nightly shows for visitors will continue for now. Jack Gough, a representative of the Invasive Species Council, called Philip Island likely the best-prepared location in Australia, but noted that vaccination should have begun earlier. Todd emphasized that the detection of the virus in the little penguin is cause for concern, but experts advise continuing the vaccination program as quickly and safely as possible. Officials are also considering expanding the program to include vulnerable animal species in captivity. analysis.brief_en: Australia has launched a program to vaccinate colonies of little penguins against the H5 strain of avian influenza, following the confirmation of a penguin's death from the virus. The initiative, reported by MercoPress on August 19, 2026, involves capturing and vaccinating over 5,000 birds on Philip Island and St. Kilda in Victoria. Operations are conducted at night when penguins return from the sea, and they are directed to a special area for vaccination and microchipping. Experts warn it could push some unique and native species to extinction. Animals The threat the H5N1 avian flu poses to Australia and New Zealand's unique wildlife August 18, 20265:25 PM ET Heard on All Things Considered By Kristina Kukolja The threat the H5N1 avian flu poses to Australia and New Zealand’s unique wildlife Listen· 2:342-Minute ListenPlaylist Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5929107/nx-s1-9892129" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript After killing millions of animals worldwide, the highly contagious H5N1 avian flu has arrived in Australia and New Zealand. Experts warn it could push some unique and native species to extinction. Transcript JUANA SUMMERS, HOST: After killing millions of animals worldwide, the highly contagious H5N1 avian flu has arrived in Australia and New Zealand. Experts warn it could push some unique and native species to extinction. Kristina Kukolja reports from Melbourne. (SOUNDBITE OF WATER LAPPING) KRISTINA KUKOLJA, BYLINE: Gentle waves lap the shore at sunset in Bayside, Melbourne, to reveal one of the city's cutest attractions. (SOUNDBITE OF PENGUIN CALLING) KUKOLJA: The breakwater at the end of the main pier is home to some 1,400 little penguins. Ecologist Tiana Preston is among experts warning the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus that's been spreading in Australia in the last several weeks could wipe out up to 40% of their colony. TIANA PRESTON: It's that sort of behavior where they're coming into contact with each other a lot that makes them particularly vulnerable. KUKOLJA: A recent Australian government assessment has found nearly 1 in 5 native birds and mammals are at high, very high or extremely high risk from the virus. Of the more than 2,000 species examined, several are already critically endangered, and, the report states, unlikely to survive infection, and hundreds are at risk of being severely depleted. CAROL BOOTH: We could have a greatly accelerated push to extinction for a lot of species. KUKOLJA: That's Carol Booth, a conservation and biosecurity policy expert with the group Invasive Species Australia. BOOTH: Eighty-seven percent of our mammals are found nowhere else and almost half our bird species, which means if we lose them here, they're gone globally. KUKOLJA: A risk acknowledged by the Australian government, which says mass wildlife deaths are now inevitable, less than two months after the first mainland case was detected. Biosecurity measures are being tightened around the country. Australia will also follow New Zealand's lead and vaccinate some native birds in captivity, says Environment Minister Murray Watt. MURRAY WATT: We're taking this step now because, of course, the situation regarding bird flu in Australia is escalating. (SOUNDBITE OF BIRD SQUEAKING) KUKOLJA: New Zealand aims to vaccinate 300 wild and captive birds from the country's five most threatened species, like the flightless nocturnal kakapo parrot. (SOUNDBITE OF PARROT SQUAWKING) KUKOLJA: Ash Murphy is a biosecurity manager with the New Zealand government's Department of Conservation. ASH MURPHY: The risk in New Zealand is some of our species are so low that a decline might be impossible to recover from. KUKOLJA: But experts say the vaccine alone is not enough to defend native species against the virus, and more needs to be done. For NPR News, I'm Kristina Kukolja in Melbourne, Australia. analysis.location_and_population: Australia and New Zealand, with a focus on native bird and mammal species, including the little penguin colony in Bayside, Melbourne.
analysis.event: The H5N1 avian flu virus has arrived in Australia and New Zealand, posing a significant threat to their unique wildlife. Experts warn that it could lead to the extinction of some native species.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: A recent Australian government assessment found nearly 1 in 5 native birds and mammals are at high, very high, or extremely high risk from the virus. Of the more than 2,000 species examined, several are already critically endangered, and hundreds are at risk of severe depletion. The virus could accelerate the extinction of species unique to these regions.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Biosecurity measures are being tightened around the country. Australia plans to follow New Zealand's lead by vaccinating some native birds in captivity. However, experts say the vaccine alone is not sufficient to defend native species against the virus.

analysis.brief_en: The H5N1 avian flu virus has arrived in Australia and New Zealand, threatening their unique wildlife. Experts warn that the virus could push some native species to extinction, with a recent Australian government assessment indicating that nearly 1 in 5 native birds and mammals are at high, very high, or extremely high risk. The virus has already affected a little penguin colony in Bayside, Melbourne, and is spreading rapidly. Conservationists emphasize that while biosecurity measures are being strengthened and vaccination programs are being considered, the vaccine alone may not be enough to protect these species. The Australian government acknowledges the risk and states that mass wildlife deaths are now inevitable, less than two months after the first mainland case was detected. The situation highlights the vulnerability of endemic species to this highly contagious pathogen.

analysis.time: The article was published on August 20, 2026. The event date is not explicitly stated in the evidence, but the cameras broke three months prior to the publication date, which would be around May 20, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event occurred at UC Berkeley, specifically involving the peregrine falcons nested on the Campanile. The affected population includes the falcons, which are birds, and the scientists and volunteers monitoring them.
analysis.event: Bird flu may have killed UC Berkeley’s falcons, as indicated by the cameras that broke three months ago. The event is reported by Cal Falcons, the organization responsible for the 24-hour livestream, and is described as a suspected cause of the falcons' deaths.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The article mentions ongoing complications with bird flu, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided. The risk is not explicitly stated, but the flu is noted as a potential threat to the falcons.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The response involves hope for the falcons' return and ongoing monitoring by scientists and volunteers. The investigation into the cause of the falcons' deaths is not fully resolved, and the status remains under investigation.

analysis.brief_en: The article from Daily Cal, published on August 20, 2026, discusses the potential impact of bird flu on UC Berkeley’s peregrine falcons, which nest on the Campanile. The cameras monitoring the falcons broke three months prior, raising concerns about their survival. Cal Falcons, the organization responsible for the 24-hour livestream, hopes to see the falcons return despite ongoing complications with bird flu. The event is reported as suspected, with no confirmed case counts or death numbers provided. The response includes monitoring efforts and hope for recovery, but the investigation into the falcons' condition remains under way. The article does not provide explicit risk levels or further details on the health effects of the bird flu on the falcons.

news.content: H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife. Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1 , a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020. Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species. While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth. An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction. Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes. Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments. Tasmanian devils are an endangered species - HANDOUT/Aussie Ark/AFP via Getty Images Dingoes are among the mammals that are unique to Australia - iStockphoto “This could be quite devastating to what is a unique ecosystem with endangered populations,” Professor Ian Brown, Head of Avian Virology at The Pirbright Institute, told The Telegraph. “It’s been a waiting game [...] I don’t think that any are that surprised that the virus has got to Australia now,” Prof Ashley C. Banyard, an avian virology expert at the government’s Animal and Plant Health Agency, said. “I think people have been expecting it [the virus] to reach Australia as several bird species that travel to that region have long-distance migratory pathways from areas where the virus has been detected previously, and we continue to detect positives on British Overseas Territories in the sub-Antarctic region where these species migrate from”, said Prof Banyard. The government is set to begin a vaccination campaign in the coming weeks to protect some of these endangered species that are conserved in captivity – beginning with rare birds like the orange-bellied parrot, the regent honeyeater, and Western Australia’s black cockatoos. “We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading amongst wild birds, but we can take action to protect the species most at risk, and the vaccination is now part of that response,” Australia’s Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in a statement on Tuesday. “Obviously, Australia wants to protect these species; they’re of high conservation concern, and they want to avoid this virus ripping through them,” said Prof Banyard. “But I think the bigger picture is how do you deal with the introductions from wild birds, which we’ve all suffered with for many years across Europe and elsewhere. “Ultimately biosecurity is essential to prevention in poultry species and with wild bird cases increasing in the region, stringent biosecurity will be critical in preventing this becoming an even bigger problem,” he added. Since 2022, H5N1 has spread at a rapid pace across the world, decimating millions of domestic and wild bird populations as well as infecting a wide range of animals, from otters to seals to lions, tigers, and bears. It has had a huge impact on the farming industry and sent the price of eggs and poultry meat soaring as flocks are culled to try to contain the spread of the virus. In Britain and the EU, almost 48 million birds were culled between 2021 and 2022 alone at the height of the bird-flu season. This risk now threatens the Australian poultry industry, which contributes roughly $4.1 billion to the regional agricultural industry every year. “It hasn’t hit poultry [in Australia] yet. If it does get into flocks, it’s always going to be problematic. But I would imagine flocks in Australia and New Zealand are quite spread apart, and so the risk of lateral spread is probably lower [than in the UK],” said Prof Banyard. The virus also poses a threat to human health, and it has long been feared that H5N1 could spark the next pandemic, should it develop the ability to spread between people. More than 1,000 people have contracted the virus since it first emerged in the late 1990s, mostly through close contact with sickened animals, almost half of whom have died. Australian authorities currently deem the risk to human health as “low”, and have invested $113 million Australian dollars (£59 million) into preparedness activities, including boosting national stockpiles of pandemic flu vaccines, should the virus gain the ability to spread person-to-person. news.content: News World In South Australia, more than a thousand terns may have died from H5N1 Lev Shevtsov 20 August 2026 07:59 Authorities in the state of South Australia have reported three instances of mass bird deaths on remote islands. In total, more than 1,000 dead crested terns were found there, which, according to preliminary estimates, may have died from H5N1 avian influenza, ABC News Australia reports. State Premier Peter Malinauskas told the South Australian Parliament that the dead birds were discovered on Wednesday. The cases were recorded on Traubridge Island near the York Peninsula, as well as on the two small islands of North Page and South Page near Kangaroo Island. For more breaking news, follow the UA.News Telegram channel . According to Malinauskas, the mass die-off was detected by the state government’s disease surveillance teams. He called the loss of more than a thousand birds deeply alarming and noted that authorities are taking these cases seriously. As of the date of this report, 177 confirmed cases of H5 avian influenza had been recorded in South Australia. The state government is also investigating a suspected case in a little penguin on Kangaroo Island. No mass deaths of mammals have been reported, and H5N1 has not been detected in poultry or livestock. Read us on Telegram and Sends Download our app

news.content_title: 1000 birds found dead in avian flu mass mortalities
news.content: 1000 birds found dead in avian flu mass mortalities Mass mortalities of crested terns have been reported in South Australia. Photo: AAP Three mass bird mortalities involving more than 1000 crested terns have been reported amid a distressing spread of avian influenza. South Australian authorities said on Thursday the coastal birds were discovered on Wednesday and were believed to have died from H5N1. Premier Peter Malinauskas told SA Parliament the deaths occurred on remote offshore islands, the ABC reports. The islands included Troubridge Island off Yorke Peninsula and two small islands off Kangaroo Island known as North Page and South Page. Another case of a dead little penguin from Kangaroo Island was also under investigation. As of Wednesday there were 236 confirmed H5 bird flu events in wild birds, with most in South Australia. Authorities have received more than 21,000 calls to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline since the outbreak began. Tasmania’s tally has jumped to 10 after four more wild birds on King Island tested positive, with two crested terns and two silver gulls found dead on beaches and bays around Currie. Authorities say the focus remains on early detection and surveillance, with crews inspecting about 760 kilometres of the state’s north-west coastline and no mass die-offs reported. In Western Australia, wildlife experts warn the virus is already creating an animal-welfare crunch as some private veterinary clinics stop accepting birds and, in some cases, other wildlife altogether. Meanwhile, hundreds of young pelicans have been found dead at Lake Cawndilla in outback NSW. However, samples have ruled out bird flu as the cause of death. Further testing is underway but authorities say it may take weeks to determine what happened to the 400 pelicans. -with AAP Want to see more stories from The New Daily in your Google search results? - Click here to set The New Daily as a preferred source. - Tick the box next to "The New Daily". NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, August 20, 2026 Louisiana DOH Reports Naegleria fowleri infection in Louisiana resident Credit CDC #19,301 Nearly every year we see a handful of rare - mostly fatal - brain infections caused by free living amoebas (Naegleria fowleri) that inhabit warm, fresh water (see A Reminder About Naegleria Season - 2019). Dubbed the `brain eating amoeba' by the press - this infection is called PAM (Primary amebic meningoencephalitis) - and occurs when the amoeba enters the brain through the nasal passages, usually due to the forceful aspiration of contaminated water into the nose. Not every PAM case is due to Naegleria, as Balamuthia mandrillaris and Acanthamoeba - and other non-Naegleria amoebic infections - can cause similar pathologies. Last year the CDC's MMWR carried a report on a fatal 2024 case from Texas, which involved a previously healthy 71-year old woman who used unsterilized water to perform nasal irrigation. This is a common way that people around the world have become infected (see 2011's Neti Pots & Naegleria Fowleri). The CDC and state health departments have long warned on the dangers of using tap water to perform nasal irrigation, and offer advice on safer alternatives. But most U.S. cases occur while swimming, often in warm stagnant freshwater lakes, rivers, canals, and ponds. Less commonly, we've seen infections attributed to water parks, private swimming pools, and even the public water supply. In 2013, in Louisiana: St. Bernard Parish Water Supply Tests Positive For Naegleria Fowleri, we saw the tragic story of a 4-year-old Mississippi child visiting a St. Bernard Parish home, who (according to this NOLA.COM report) appears to have contracted the amoeba while playing with a water hose and a slip-and-slide. Five years ago we looked at an MMWR: Epidemiological Investigation Into A Case Of Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis in California which suggested a poorly chlorinated spring-fed swimming pool was the likely source of infection and death of a 21 year old woman. In 2013, in Arkansas: Naegleria fowleri Shuts Water Park, we saw the second suspected case in 3 years from the same recreational venue. Only 3 or 4 cases are reported in the United States each summer, but in 2017 a research letter written by epidemiologists at the CDC (see EID Journal: Estimation of Undiagnosed Naegleria fowleri (PAM), United States) estimated the yearly number PAM cases in the United States probably averages closer to 16 (8 males, 8 females). Meaning that 70%-80% likely go unrecognized. But even so, your odds of contracting PAM are exceedingly low. Louisiana Health Department report follows: LDH reports Naegleria fowleri infection in Louisiana resident Rare infection most likely acquired while swimming in Lake Claiborne Baton Rouge, Louisiana, Aug 19, 2026 - The Louisiana Department of Health is reporting a confirmed Naegleria fowleri infection in a Louisiana resident. The resident most likely acquired the infection while swimming in Lake Claiborne, located in Claiborne Parish, shortly before illness. Naegleria fowleri, often referred to as a brain-eating amoeba, is commonly found in warm freshwater lakes, rivers, canals, and ponds throughout the United States. It can cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a brain infection that may result when water containing the amoeba rushes up the nose and reaches the brain. The infection is extremely rare, but nearly always fatal. Naegleria fowleri cannot infect people if swallowed and is not spread from person to person. The amoeba is not found in salt water or in properly maintained and chlorinated pools. Symptoms of Naegleria fowleri infection typically start with severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting and progress to stiff neck, seizures, and coma that can lead to death. Symptoms usually begin about five days after infection but can start within one to 12 days. Naegleria fowleri thrives in warm, fresh water and grows best at higher temperatures up to 115°F. The amoeba is naturally occurring, and there is no routine environmental test for Naegleria fowleri in bodies of water. A Health Alert Network (HAN) was shared to all state providers from Louisiana Department of Health on August 18, 2026, advising on symptoms and reporting. Though the risk of infection is low, recreational water users should always assume there is a risk when they enter warm fresh water. You can reduce your risk of infection by limiting the amount of water that goes up the nose. Recommended precautions include: Use caution when engaging in water-related activities in warm freshwater during periods of extended extreme heat. Naegleria fowleri usually occurs when temperatures increase for prolonged periods, resulting in higher water temperatures and lower water levels. Swimmers can reduce their risk by keeping their heads out of the water and using nose clips or plugging their noses when going underwater. Avoid submersing your head in hot springs and other untreated fresh thermal water. Avoid digging in or stirring up the sediment while taking part in water-related activities in shallow, warm freshwater areas. ​Naegleria fowleri infections are rare, with only 180 known cases of PAM in the U.S. (between zero and eight cases annually) from 1937 through 2025. Louisiana had three Naegleria fowleri cases during that time period. For more information regarding Naegleria fowleri, please visit Naegleria fowleri Infections | Naegleria fowleri Infection | CDC. For more information on the Naegleria parasite, you can also visit the CDC’s Naegleria webpage. Australia: Media Reports of Multiple Mass Mortality Events in Birds (H5N1 Suspected) Data as of 4pm AEST, 19 August 2026 #19,300 While HPAI H5N1 reporting from governmental sources have slowed in recent days, overnight the Australian press reported on multiple mass mortality events involving birds in South Australia and Tasmania (see ABC News Bird flu suspected after more than 1,000 birds found dead in SA, more deaths in Tasmania). According to multiple news sources (see here and here), South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas addressed the SA parliament (Aug 20th) to announce that more than 1,000 crested terns had died across three mass mortality events on several remote offshore islands. Additionally there are reports of > 2 dozen dead penguins in Tasmania. While H5N1 has not been confirmed, HPAI is strongly suspected. For now, there are no reports of H5N1 in non-avian wildlife, poultry, or livestock. While we await further details (and/or confirmation) we've two other sources of background information; an expert commentary from Australia's National Testing laboratory CSIRO, and a series of academic analyses from The Conversation. Thursday, August 20, 2026 Louisiana DOH Reports Naegleria fowleri infection in Louisiana resident Credit CDC #19,301 Nearly every year we see a handful of rare - mostly fatal - brain infections caused by free living amoebas (Naegleria fowleri) that inhabit warm, fresh water (see A Reminder About Naegleria Season - 2019). Dubbed the `brain eating amoeba' by the press - this infection is called PAM (Primary amebic meningoencephalitis) - and occurs when the amoeba enters the brain through the nasal passages, usually due to the forceful aspiration of contaminated water into the nose. Not every PAM case is due to Naegleria, as Balamuthia mandrillaris and Acanthamoeba - and other non-Naegleria amoebic infections - can cause similar pathologies. Last year the CDC's MMWR carried a report on a fatal 2024 case from Texas, which involved a previously healthy 71-year old woman who used unsterilized water to perform nasal irrigation. This is a common way that people around the world have become infected (see 2011's Neti Pots & Naegleria Fowleri). The CDC and state health departments have long warned on the dangers of using tap water to perform nasal irrigation, and offer advice on safer alternatives. But most U.S. cases occur while swimming, often in warm stagnant freshwater lakes, rivers, canals, and ponds. Less commonly, we've seen infections attributed to water parks, private swimming pools, and even the public water supply. In 2013, in Louisiana: St. Bernard Parish Water Supply Tests Positive For Naegleria Fowleri, we saw the tragic story of a 4-year-old Mississippi child visiting a St. Bernard Parish home, who (according to this NOLA.COM report) appears to have contracted the amoeba while playing with a water hose and a slip-and-slide. Five years ago we looked at an MMWR: Epidemiological Investigation Into A Case Of Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis in California which suggested a poorly chlorinated spring-fed swimming pool was the likely source of infection and death of a 21 year old woman. In 2013, in Arkansas: Naegleria fowleri Shuts Water Park, we saw the second suspected case in 3 years from the same recreational venue. Only 3 or 4 cases are reported in the United States each summer, but in 2017 a research letter written by epidemiologists at the CDC (see EID Journal: Estimation of Undiagnosed Naegleria fowleri (PAM), United States) estimated the yearly number PAM cases in the United States probably averages closer to 16 (8 males, 8 females). Meaning that 70%-80% likely go unrecognized. But even so, your odds of contracting PAM are exceedingly low. Louisiana Health Department report follows: LDH reports Naegleria fowleri infection in Louisiana resident Rare infection most likely acquired while swimming in Lake Claiborne Baton Rouge, Louisiana, Aug 19, 2026 - The Louisiana Department of Health is reporting a confirmed Naegleria fowleri infection in a Louisiana resident. The resident most likely acquired the infection while swimming in Lake Claiborne, located in Claiborne Parish, shortly before illness. Naegleria fowleri, often referred to as a brain-eating amoeba, is commonly found in warm freshwater lakes, rivers, canals, and ponds throughout the United States. It can cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a brain infection that may result when water containing the amoeba rushes up the nose and reaches the brain. The infection is extremely rare, but nearly always fatal. Naegleria fowleri cannot infect people if swallowed and is not spread from person to person. The amoeba is not found in salt water or in properly maintained and chlorinated pools. Symptoms of Naegleria fowleri infection typically start with severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting and progress to stiff neck, seizures, and coma that can lead to death. Symptoms usually begin about five days after infection but can start within one to 12 days. Naegleria fowleri thrives in warm, fresh water and grows best at higher temperatures up to 115°F. The amoeba is naturally occurring, and there is no routine environmental test for Naegleria fowleri in bodies of water. A Health Alert Network (HAN) was shared to all state providers from Louisiana Department of Health on August 18, 2026, advising on symptoms and reporting. Though the risk of infection is low, recreational water users should always assume there is a risk when they enter warm fresh water. You can reduce your risk of infection by limiting the amount of water that goes up the nose. Recommended precautions include: Use caution when engaging in water-related activities in warm freshwater during periods of extended extreme heat. Naegleria fowleri usually occurs when temperatures increase for prolonged periods, resulting in higher water temperatures and lower water levels. Swimmers can reduce their risk by keeping their heads out of the water and using nose clips or plugging their noses when going underwater. Avoid submersing your head in hot springs and other untreated fresh thermal water. Avoid digging in or stirring up the sediment while taking part in water-related activities in shallow, warm freshwater areas. ​Naegleria fowleri infections are rare, with only 180 known cases of PAM in the U.S. (between zero and eight cases annually) from 1937 through 2025. Louisiana had three Naegleria fowleri cases during that time period. For more information regarding Naegleria fowleri, please visit Naegleria fowleri Infections | Naegleria fowleri Infection | CDC. For more information on the Naegleria parasite, you can also visit the CDC’s Naegleria webpage. Thursday, August 20, 2026 Louisiana DOH Reports Naegleria fowleri infection in Louisiana resident Credit CDC #19,301 Nearly every year we see a handful of rare - mostly fatal - brain infections caused by free living amoebas (Naegleria fowleri) that inhabit warm, fresh water (see A Reminder About Naegleria Season - 2019). Dubbed the `brain eating amoeba' by the press - this infection is called PAM (Primary amebic meningoencephalitis) - and occurs when the amoeba enters the brain through the nasal passages, usually due to the forceful aspiration of contaminated water into the nose. Not every PAM case is due to Naegleria, as Balamuthia mandrillaris and Acanthamoeba - and other non-Naegleria amoebic infections - can cause similar pathologies. Last year the CDC's MMWR carried a report on a fatal 2024 case from Texas, which involved a previously healthy 71-year old woman who used unsterilized water to perform nasal irrigation. This is a common way that people around the world have become infected (see 2011's Neti Pots & Naegleria Fowleri). The CDC and state health departments have long warned on the dangers of using tap water to perform nasal irrigation, and offer advice on safer alternatives. But most U.S. cases occur while swimming, often in warm stagnant freshwater lakes, rivers, canals, and ponds. Less commonly, we've seen infections attributed to water parks, private swimming pools, and even the public water supply. In 2013, in Louisiana: St. Bernard Parish Water Supply Tests Positive For Naegleria Fowleri, we saw the tragic story of a 4-year-old Mississippi child visiting a St. Bernard Parish home, who (according to this NOLA.COM report) appears to have contracted the amoeba while playing with a water hose and a slip-and-slide. Five years ago we looked at an MMWR: Epidemiological Investigation Into A Case Of Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis in California which suggested a poorly chlorinated spring-fed swimming pool was the likely source of infection and death of a 21 year old woman. In 2013, in Arkansas: Naegleria fowleri Shuts Water Park, we saw the second suspected case in 3 years from the same recreational venue. Only 3 or 4 cases are reported in the United States each summer, but in 2017 a research letter written by epidemiologists at the CDC (see EID Journal: Estimation of Undiagnosed Naegleria fowleri (PAM), United States) estimated the yearly number PAM cases in the United States probably averages closer to 16 (8 males, 8 females). Meaning that 70%-80% likely go unrecognized. But even so, your odds of contracting PAM are exceedingly low. Louisiana Health Department report follows: LDH reports Naegleria fowleri infection in Louisiana resident Rare infection most likely acquired while swimming in Lake Claiborne Baton Rouge, Louisiana, Aug 19, 2026 - The Louisiana Department of Health is reporting a confirmed Naegleria fowleri infection in a Louisiana resident. The resident most likely acquired the infection while swimming in Lake Claiborne, located in Claiborne Parish, shortly before illness. Naegleria fowleri, often referred to as a brain-eating amoeba, is commonly found in warm freshwater lakes, rivers, canals, and ponds throughout the United States. It can cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a brain infection that may result when water containing the amoeba rushes up the nose and reaches the brain. The infection is extremely rare, but nearly always fatal. Naegleria fowleri cannot infect people if swallowed and is not spread from person to person. The amoeba is not found in salt water or in properly maintained and chlorinated pools. Symptoms of Naegleria fowleri infection typically start with severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting and progress to stiff neck, seizures, and coma that can lead to death. Symptoms usually begin about five days after infection but can start within one to 12 days. Naegleria fowleri thrives in warm, fresh water and grows best at higher temperatures up to 115°F. The amoeba is naturally occurring, and there is no routine environmental test for Naegleria fowleri in bodies of water. A Health Alert Network (HAN) was shared to all state providers from Louisiana Department of Health on August 18, 2026, advising on symptoms and reporting. Though the risk of infection is low, recreational water users should always assume there is a risk when they enter warm fresh water. You can reduce your risk of infection by limiting the amount of water that goes up the nose. Recommended precautions include: Use caution when engaging in water-related activities in warm freshwater during periods of extended extreme heat. Naegleria fowleri usually occurs when temperatures increase for prolonged periods, resulting in higher water temperatures and lower water levels. Swimmers can reduce their risk by keeping their heads out of the water and using nose clips or plugging their noses when going underwater. Avoid submersing your head in hot springs and other untreated fresh thermal water. Avoid digging in or stirring up the sediment while taking part in water-related activities in shallow, warm freshwater areas. ​Naegleria fowleri infections are rare, with only 180 known cases of PAM in the U.S. (between zero and eight cases annually) from 1937 through 2025. Louisiana had three Naegleria fowleri cases during that time period. For more information regarding Naegleria fowleri, please visit Naegleria fowleri Infections | Naegleria fowleri Infection | CDC. For more information on the Naegleria parasite, you can also visit the CDC’s Naegleria webpage. Australia: Media Reports of Multiple Mass Mortality Events in Birds (H5N1 Suspected) Data as of 4pm AEST, 19 August 2026 #19,300 While HPAI H5N1 reporting from governmental sources have slowed in recent days, overnight the Australian press reported on multiple mass mortality events involving birds in South Australia and Tasmania (see ABC News Bird flu suspected after more than 1,000 birds found dead in SA, more deaths in Tasmania). According to multiple news sources (see here and here), South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas addressed the SA parliament (Aug 20th) to announce that more than 1,000 crested terns had died across three mass mortality events on several remote offshore islands. Additionally there are reports of > 2 dozen dead penguins in Tasmania. While H5N1 has not been confirmed, HPAI is strongly suspected. For now, there are no reports of H5N1 in non-avian wildlife, poultry, or livestock. While we await further details (and/or confirmation) we've two other sources of background information; an expert commentary from Australia's National Testing laboratory CSIRO, and a series of academic analyses from The Conversation. First this analysis from CSIRO (h/t Pathfinder on FluTrackers): Expert Commentary: What do we know about H5 bird flu? 18 AUGUST 2026 4 MIN READ In June 2026, Australia recorded its first cases of the highly contagious H5 bird flu. As Australia's national reference laboratory for animal diseases, CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) plays a critical role in protecting Australia's valuable livestock and aquaculture industries and the wider community from infectious diseases such as bird flu. Scientists at ACDP have been conducting testing and genetic analysis to learn more about exactly which strain of the virus has arrived on our shores, and how it is spreading. All quotes below are available for use by media. Spokespeople quoted: Dr Frank Wong, Senior Research Scientist at CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness. Dr Wong is also a World Organization for Animal Health-designated reference expert on avian influenza Dr Matt Neave, Team Leader of Sequencing and Agent Characterisation at CSIRO's ACDP Dr Debbie Eagles, Director of CSIRO's ACDP. What is H5N1 and why is it a concern? Dr Frank Wong: For the past 5 or 6 years the world has been affected by a bird flu panzootic. This is what we call a pandemic in animals. In this case, because the virus is an avian virus, it has mostly impacted birds around the world. The clade 2.3.4.4b lineage of H5N1 is a highly pathogenic bird flu virus that emerged around 2020-2021, first spreading across Europe and then moving on to other continents, including Asia and North America. Along the way it has caused mass mortalities in both domestic poultry as well as many species of wild bird. H5N1 has been able to spread rapidly across different continents largely due its ability to be sustained in migratory wild birds, like waterfowl such as ducks and geese. The genotype that we're talking about for Australia, known as genotype B3.2, arose from reassortment in North America and then spread to South America and the sub-Antarctic islands. It had a great impact on South American poultry industries as well as wild bird life and marine mammals, so that's why we're concerned about the introduction of the virus to Australia. What does ACDP's genetic testing show us? Dr Matt Neave: Sequencing the virus genome has become really important in disease outbreaks like this one. We're now able to do it much quicker than in the past and can get a whole influenza genome in around 15 to 26 hours. From the viral genome we are able to determine several important things, including the exact strain of the virus. Another thing we can do is compare that viral genome to other reference sequences in our database or public databases online. This allows us to determine how closely related our Australian cases are to the sub-Antarctic ones, for example. Our testing shows us that the sequences from the first two cases in Australia were closely related to ones from Heard Island. From the data we have at hand, it appears Heard Island is the most likely source of the Australian infections. By comparing genetic sequences from virus samples, scientists can trace the relationships between the first Australian H5 bird flu cases and those detected on Heard Island. Credit: Matthew J. Neave et al. Show image description (Follow link to read the full report). Although there are now roughly 2 dozen entries, going back to H5N1's arrival in Australia in mid-June, over the past few days these 4 essays have been published. Published: August 20, 2026 The first wave of bird flu is the worst: what Australia can learn from overseas Bethany J Hoye, University of Wollongong The rest of the world has already had to grapple with bird flu – and there are lessons for Australia. Published: August 18, 2026 More than 5,000 little penguins will be vaxxed against bird flu. How will this protect them? Julie Old, Western Sydney University Little penguins are flightless and return at night to the same burrow, making it easier to capture and vaccinate them. Published: August 17, 2026 From the coasts to the plains, bird flu could threaten not just birds – but their homes Penny Olsen, Australian National University From raucous honeyeaters to top predators, Australia’s birds are vital to nature. Published: August 16, 2026 Is bird flu infecting humans? How would we know? Allen Cheng, Monash University Even with bird flu circulating in Australia, the risk to humans is low. But some groups are still at increased risk. Wednesday, August 19, 2026 WHO Influenza at the human-animal interface (Aug 7th) - Uptick in H9N2 Cases in China #19,299 The WHO has released an update (dated Aug 7th, but posted overnight) of human novel flu infections reported between July 8th and Aug 7th. Included are 8 H9N2 cases from Mainland China, and 1 H5N1 case from Cambodia (all previously reported). This report also confirms the H5 case reported from Bangladesh in July has been confirmed as H5N1. For reasons well above my pay grade, reporting from Hong Kong's CHP on H9N2 cases has been a bit chaotic this month (reporting the same 4 recent cases as `new' for the past 3 weeks running), and the WHO's weekly WPRO avian flu report hasn't been updated since Aug 7th. What we can say, however, is that China (along with a recent case in Hong Kong) has seen an uptick in reported H9N2 cases this summer. Whether this is due to more frequent spillovers, or better surveillance, isn't known. Despite being clearly zoonotic - LPAI H9N2 is considered a `non-reportable' disease in poultry or wild birds by WOAH (see Terrestrial Animal Code). Complicating matters, China's attempts to control LPAI H9N2 through vaccines have been less than successful. In 2025's NPJ Vaccines: Impact of Inactivated Vaccine on Transmission and Evolution of H9N2 Avian Influenza Virus in Chickens, we saw evidence that inactivated vaccines failed to prevent - or even reduce - H9N2 in China's poultry, and may have driven viral evolution (including mammalian adaptations). Several recent Chinese studies have found signs that LPAI H9N2 is becoming better adapted to mammals, warning of its pandemic potential; including: Two weeks ago, in EM&I: Genetic evolution, phylodynamics, geographic spread of H9N2 avian influenza viruses in China from 2014 to 2025: an increasing potential zoonotic risk, we saw yet another Chinese study warning that H9N2 was accruing mammalian adaptations which increases its zoonotic risk. Two months ago, in Viruses: Epidemiological and Virological Characteristics of H9N2 Avian Influenza Virus in Jiangsu Province, China, 2024, researchers warned that that Jiangsu’s circulating H9N2 viruses have acquired human receptor preference and mammalian adaptation, posing silent infection and pandemic risks Last October, in China CDC Weekly: Epidemiological and Genetic Characterization of Three H9N2 Viruses Causing Human Infections, investigators reported a number of indicators of increased mammalian adaptation within the virus, including an enhanced ability to infect upper respiratory (α2,6-sialic acid) tract receptors, and a number of HA protein mutations, including; H191N, A198V, Q226L, and Q234L. The Asian Y280/G57 lineages have shown increasing signs of mammalian adaptation (see EM&I: Enhanced Replication of a Contemporary Avian Influenza A H9N2 Virus in Human Respiratory Organoids)), while the African and Middle Eastern Lineages (mostly European G1-like) are older and less evolved. Last summer, in Nature: Genetic diversity of H9N2 avian influenza viruses in poultry across China and implications for zoonotic transmission, researchers reported rising prevalence of key mutations associated with increased infectivity and pathogenicity in mammals. While H9N2 doesn't garner the kind of headlines that H5N1 gets, our own CDC lists two lineages (A(H9N2) G1 and A(H9N2) Y280) as having at least some pandemic potential, and several candidate vaccines have been developed. In terms of risk of emergence, the H9N2 Y280 lineage is ranked higher than H5N1 Which is why any uptick in activity is worthy of our attention. Australia H5N1 Update #19,298 It's been a week since Australia Changed How They Report H5N1 - reporting `events' rather than individual detections in wildlife - and while the numbers have continued to rise (see below), we seem to be getting fewer (and less detailed) updates. In the first 10 days of August, Australia's Chief Veterinary Officer released 11 bird flu updates/statements, but has only released one in the past 9 days. Similarly, Victoria's last update was August 15th. Up until a week ago, DAFF was reporting both the number of positive and negative test results, along with number hotline reports (see below). This gave us some idea of the percentage of hotline reports being investigated (roughly 1 in 13). (Aug 13th DAFF) With the move towards only tracking `events', that metric is no longer provided. While I'd certainly like more data, there is only so much that any country can reasonably do when they are faced with a highly aggressive pathogen like avian H5N1. For now, South Australia continues to post detailed daily updates, but added the following notice this week: Thus far, H5N1 has not been detected in poultry, livestock, or non-avian wildlife. But how long that reassuring status quo can last is unknown. Tuesday, August 18, 2026 Preprint: Enhanced Pathogenicity and Contact Transmissibility of Human-origin Avian Influenza H5N1 Clade 2.3.4.4b Genotype B3.13 Compared to D1.1 in Ferrets #19,297 The two main H5N1 genotypes (out of > 100) we are watching in the United States are the B3.13 `Bovine' strain which emerged in Texas Cattle in early 2024, and the D1.1 avian strain that appeared in Canada the following fall and quickly spread through wild birds and poultry across the continent. From a distance, it appears that the B3.13 strain produces mainly mild illness in humans (ie. conjunctivitis), while the D1.1 strain has been linked to a number of severe illnesses and several deaths. But appearances, particularly when surveillance and testing are limited, can be deceiving. Bovine B3.13 H5N1 infections are probably easier to track because they occur on dairy farms, are more likely to be treated with antivirals, and may be more likely due to `splash' events where infection occurs through the ocular route. While many D1.1 infections occur on poultry farms, it may also be encountered by the general public through contact with wild birds and/or backyard poultry, which makes it more difficult to track. Complicating matters, we've seen a number of head-to-head comparison studies (see here, here, and here) that have provided differing assessments of the transmissibility and virulence of these two genotypes. In one study using human nasal and airway organoids, D1.1 appeared to be better adapted to human physiology, while in another (see IJID study) B3.13 caused severe disease, extra-respiratory spread, and lethality in ferrets while D1.1 caused milder disease with no lethality. To be fair, differences in methods and materials used…
